notes.text:
The note was seven words. My work is done. Why wait?

It was a bookkeeper's sentence, and he knew exactly what stood on the books. The work had never been the company. It was the promise on the box: you press the button, we do the rest. In 1877 a photograph had required a wagonload of glass and chemistry and a tent; by 1932 the camera was in the house, the album was on the shelf, and pressing the button was something a child did without thinking. Below that entry sat the rest of it: the machine for keeping the promise, thirteen hundred acres of it; the laboratory that would deliver the color he had chased for thirty years, three years too late for him to see it; a city with his name over its doors and a school in Boston without it. What remained, running the company, defending the margins, riding out the Depression, was other men's work, of a kind he had spent thirty years training them to do. There was no heir on the ledger, because the ledger was the heir. He had audited his own life the way he had audited everything since he was nineteen, found the accounts in balance, and closed them.

before.text: George Eastman invented the user. Not the camera, which existed, and not flexible film, which cost him five million dollars to be told he had not invented. What he built in 1888 was a customer who had never existed: an ordinary person, with no chemistry and no darkroom, who could keep a piece of their own life. *You press the button, we do the rest.* It was the first true consumer company in America, and the promise was so complete that the man behind it disappeared into it. He removed himself from the product, from his gifts, from his own authorized biography, and finally from the world, on a March afternoon in 1932, with the alternative covered and a second pistol in the bookcase. The company he left ran on his instructions for eighty years without the judgment that wrote them. It gave the United States its eyes over the Soviet Union, put the first photograph of the Earth in front of humanity, and then, in a single year, 1976, invented the digital image, patented the sensor every phone now carries, licensed it out to the world, and chose to collect rent instead of build. It died as the man it began by firing: George Selden, the patent attorney who held paper instead of making things. In 2012 the last roll came off a machine that had run a hundred and one years, and the arsenal built to cover every avenue was sold to Apple and Google for a fifth of asking. Kodak was the only monument Eastman had. He had no children and no heirs; four biographies were commissioned by his own company and none was allowed out; the one he authorized he edited himself, and it ends in ascending triumph because it was published two years before he shot himself. Now the company is gone as well, and what survives is a slide in a business school deck about an incumbent too stupid to see digital coming, which is not what happened. This book is the first honest accounting of him, and it can only be written now, because the image has finally left matter altogether. No lens, no light, no referent. Development brought out what light had already written; the models bring out what was never there. Same verb, same dark. For the first time since 1888 the arc is complete, and you can stand at the end of the thing Eastman started and see all of it, including the parts he arranged for you not to see.

before.passage: The company he left ran on his instructions for eighty years without the judgment that wrote them. It gave the United States its eyes over the Soviet Union, put the first photograph of the Earth in front of humanity, and then, in a single year, 1976, invented the digital image, patented the color filter every phone sensor now uses, licensed it out to the world, and chose to collect rent instead of build. It ended as the man it began by firing: **George Selden**, the patent attorney Eastman let go in 1887 for being a man who held paper rather than made things, who then kept a gasoline-engine application alive for sixteen years by amendment and collected a fee on every automobile built in America until Henry Ford broke him in court in 1911. On October 23, 2012, the last roll came off a machine that had run a hundred and one years. Two months later the arsenal built to cover every avenue was sold for a fifth of asking to Apple and Google, which had inherited the position Kodak held for a century. **Kodak was the Apple and Google of its day, and it was liquidated into them.**

notes.chunk_at_written: George Eastman did not invent the camera. He invented the customer. Before 1888, photography meant chemistry, glass plates, and a darkroom. His promise, *you press the button, we do the rest*, created a person who had not previously existed: an ordinary human being who could keep a piece of their own life. By 1900 he was selling a camera to children for a dollar. Then his advertising taught the world what to photograph, inventing the vacation snapshot, the baby picture, Christmas morning, and selling the film for all three. He did not only build the machinery of memory. He built the habit, and the habit is why you have a shoebox or a hard drive.
